passages.original: sub eisdem generibus continent.urqusecunque aequivoce prædicantur.Quam vim,nisi prius de generibus, speciebus,propriis et differentiis notitiam scientiamque perceperis, nullo nunquam tempore discernis. Idem Aristoteles ait quid sint primæ substantiæ,quid secundae,et primas substantias dicit esse individuorum corporum et singulorum, ut est Cicero, aut Plato,aut Socrates. Secundas vero substantias species appellavit, ut est homo; vel genera in quibus ipsae species continentur,ut est animal.Hæc igitur nisi prælibata generis specieique cognitione sciri non possunt.Idem ait substantiam ab alia substantia, in eo quod substantia sit, nulla differentia disgregari.
passages.english: are contained under the same genera, whatever things are predicated equivocally. You will never at any time discern this force unless you have first acquired knowledge and understanding of genera, species, properties and differences. The same Aristotle says what primary substances are and what secondary ones are, and he says that primary substances are those of individual and single bodies, such as Cicero, or Plato, or Socrates. Secondary substances he called the species, such as man, or the genera in which these species are contained, such as animal. These things therefore cannot be known unless knowledge of genus and species has been tasted beforehand. The same [Aristotle] says that a substance is separated from another substance, insofar as it is substance, by no difference.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the opening clause continues 'it is established that never…' from the preceding context. 'urqusecunque' read as 'utquaecunque'/'quaecunque'; the syntax of the first sentence is uncertain.

passages.original: Idem substantiae proprietates requirit, ut quasi impresso aliquo signo, sic proprietate nota, facilius quid substantia sit invenire atque expedire possimus. Atque hoc idem in accidentibus fecit. Nam et quantitatis et qualitatis et ad aliquid relationis propria collegit,et idem magna apud Aristotelem cura diligentiaqueconspicitur.Videsneutsesequinqueharum rerum vis in categoriasinterserat,etpraedicamentorum virtutibus inseparabiliter colligetur? Non mendax igitur Porpbyrius dehaccognitione,harum quinque rerum nobis in categorias, utilitate promisit.
passages.english: The same [Aristotle] inquires into the properties of substance, so that, as if by some sign impressed, so by a known property, we may more easily discover and set out what substance is. And he did the same in the case of accidents. For he collected the properties of quantity and of quality and of the relation 'to something', and the same is seen in Aristotle with great care and diligence. Do you see how the force of these five things inserts itself into the categories and is inseparably bound up with the powers of the predicaments? Porphyry, then, was not lying about this knowledge when he promised us [its] usefulness of these five things for the categories.
passages.notes: Run-together words separated (e.g. 'Videsne ut sese quinque harum rerum vis in categorias interserat'). The last sentence is syntactically awkward in the Latin ('de hac cognitione… utilitate'); text may be corrupt.

passages.original: Sic igitur mens rerum nixa primordiis altiori atqueincorporabiliintelligentiasubiimalur.Hinc ergo animus non solum per sensibilia res incorporales intelligendi est artifex,sed etiam fingendi sibi atque etiam mentiendi.Inde enimexformaequiethominis falsam centaurorum speciem sibi ipsa intelligentia comparavit.Has igitur mentis considerationes,quæ a rerum sensu ad intelligentiam profectæ,vel intelliguntur,vel certe figuntur, Φαντασίας Græci dicunt, generibus.speciebus et cæteris quaerunt,utrum haec vere subsistentia,et quodammodo essentiaconstan- taque intelligantur, ut a corporibus singulis vere atque integre ductam hominis speciem intelligamus, an certe quadam animi imaginatione fingant!lr, ut ille Horatii versus est: Rumano capiticervicem pictor equinam jungeresi velit, quod neque est, neque esse poterit,sed sola falsa mentis consideratione fingitur. Nimis acuta et subtilis inquisitio,atque adrem maxime profutura.Scienda enim sunt,utrum vere sint : nee esset de his disputatio consideratioque si non sint.
passages.english: Thus, then, the mind, resting on the first beginnings of things, is raised up to a higher and incorporeal understanding. Hence, therefore, the mind is skilled not only at understanding incorporeal things through sensible ones, but also at fashioning [things] for itself and even at feigning them. For from the form of a horse and of a man the understanding itself has put together for itself the false appearance of centaurs. These considerations of the mind, then, which, having set out from the sense of things toward understanding, are either understood or else fashioned, the Greeks call phantasiai [mental images]; [and] they ask about genera, species and the rest whether these are understood as truly subsisting and in a way as established in essence, so that we understand the species of man as truly and wholly drawn from individual bodies, or whether they are rather fashioned by some imagination of the mind, as in that verse of Horace: 'If a painter wished to join a horse's neck to a human head', which neither is nor could be, but is fashioned by a false consideration of the mind alone. [This is] a very sharp and subtle inquiry, and one that will be of the greatest use for the matter. For it must be known whether they truly exist; nor would there be discussion and consideration of them if they did not exist.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'sublimatur', 'fingantur', 'Humano capiti cervicem pictor equinam jungere si velit' (Horace, Ars Poetica 1). The clause 'generibus, speciebus et ceteris quaerunt' lacks a connective; 'de' seems implied. 'figuntur' read as 'finguntur'.

passages.original: Haec se igitur lacere Porphyrius pollicitus, breviter mediocriterque super his rebus tractare promittit, habita in res alias consideratione aut conjectura, quod simile est ac si diceret : Quoniam haec ad praediramenta et ad definitiones,et ad Jivisiones,et ad probationes pertinentjideohsectractalurusassumo, et eatenus de his disseram, quatenus supradictis rebus proficiunt, non quatenus de his ipsis generi- bus speciebusque, et cæteris quaevis tractari possint.Sunt enim illa (ut ipse ail) gravioris tractatus, quam doctrinam a Peripateticis acceptam,id est ab Aristotelicis,se sequi confessus est. Nam Stoiciqui de his quoque rebus tractare voluerunt, non ommino a Porphyrio suscipiuntur,atque ideo ait se a Peripateticis rationem disputationis accipere.Tunc me Fabius ita percunctatus: Quid est,inquit,quod dudum dixeras, cum a te de incorporalibus tractaretur,esse quasdam incorporalitates quæ circa corpus semper constiterent,ut sunt primæ incorporalitates post terminos ?
passages.english: Porphyry, then, having undertaken to pass over these things in silence, promises to treat these matters briefly and moderately, with regard paid to other things, or conjecture; which is as if he said: 'Since these things pertain to the predicaments, and to definitions, and to divisions, and to proofs, I therefore take them up to treat, and I shall discuss them so far as they are useful for the things mentioned above, not so far as anything whatever could be treated concerning these genera and species and the rest themselves.' For those matters, as he himself says, belong to a weightier treatise; and he has acknowledged that he follows the teaching received from the Peripatetics, that is, from the Aristotelians. For the Stoics, who also wished to treat these matters, are not at all accepted by Porphyry, and therefore he says that he takes the method of discussion from the Peripatetics. Then Fabius questioned me thus: 'What is it,' he said, 'that you said a while ago, when you were treating incorporeal things, that there are certain incorporealities which always exist around body, such as the first incorporealities after the limits?'
passages.notes: 'lacere' read as 'tacere' (to pass over in silence); 'habita in res alias consideratione aut conjectura' is unclear in sense. Fabius is the interlocutor of the dialogue.

passages.original: Addit autem ipse quod soli Latinas linguae congruere possit: dicit enim secundo modo genus dici,ut est genus causae honestum: quae generacausarum Graeci in rhetorica arte genera esse non putant, sed σχήματα vocant, id est figuras.Genera autem sola principaliaaccipiunt, demonstrativum,deliberativum etjudiciale. Quae ipsa εἴδη rhetorices vocant,id est species rhetoricae, genera vero causarum non dicimus.Tertium vero genus est id quod Porphyrius ponit, id est sub quo differentiis|distributæ species supponuntur.Sed quoniam de tertio genere tractaturus est,Victorini culpam,vel,si ita contingit,emendationem aequi bonique faciamus. Nunc ergo ad priorem apud Victorinum generis significationem revertamur,et ejus ut sunt verbaenodandaatqueexplanandasumanus.Genusnamque, inquit, diciturquorumdam ad seinvi- cem etadaliquemquodammodoseihabentiumcollectio.
passages.english: He himself adds [a sense] which can fit the Latin language alone: for he says that genus is spoken of in a second way, as in 'the honourable genus of a case'. These genera of cases the Greeks, in the art of rhetoric, do not consider genera, but call them schēmata, that is, figures. They accept as genera only the principal ones: demonstrative, deliberative and judicial. These they call the eidē of rhetoric, that is, species of rhetoric, but we do not call them genera of cases. The third genus is that which Porphyry posits, that is, under which species distributed by differences are placed. But since he is going to treat the third genus, let us take in good part the fault of Victorinus, or, if it so happens, his correction. Now, therefore, let us return to the earlier signification of genus in Victorinus, and let us undertake to untangle and explain his words as they stand. For genus, he says, is called the collection of certain things that are in some way related to one another and to some one [thing].
passages.notes: The final sentences were run together in the scan and have been separated. The last clauses ('Victorini culpam… emendationem') are somewhat obscure.

passages.original: Eorum quæ dicuntur, alia ad unitatem dicuntur, sicut sunt omnia individua, ut est Socrates, et hoc ei illud. Alia quae ad multitudinem, ut sunt genera, spe-cies, et differentiæ, et propria, et accidentia. Hxc enim communiter non unius propriseappellationis sunt Est enirn genus ut animal, species ut homo, differentia ut rationale.pJ'oprium ut risibile, accidens ut album, sedere.
passages.english: Of the things that are predicated, some are predicated of a single thing, as are all individuals, for example Socrates, and "this" and "that". Others are predicated of a multitude, as are genera, species, differences, properties and accidents. For these belong in common [to many], and are not the proper appellation of one [thing]. For a genus is, for example, animal; a species, man; a difference, rational; a property, capable of laughing; an accident, white, sitting.
passages.notes: "et hoc ei illud" read as "et hoc et illud", as in the following unit; "propriseappellationis" read as "propriae appellationis"; "pJ'oprium" read as "proprium".

passages.original: Ergo siqua accidentiavenerintabindividuis, et ea tracta in speciebusconsederint,ad ipsa quoque accidentia dici poterit genus. Quid est enim ambulans, siquis interroget: merito animal dicitur. Nihil enim ambulare nisi animal potest. Porro autem sub speciebus individua sunt, ut Cicero et Virgilius sub bomine, ad quae individua genus speciei praedicari potest. Nam si interrogaveris, quid est Cicero ? merito animal dicas. Genus igitur et ad speciem et ad differentias, et ad accidentia, et ad propria, et ad individua nominatur.
passages.english: Therefore, if any accidents come from individuals and, having been drawn [from them], settle in species, genus can also be said of these accidents themselves. For if someone asks, 'What is walking?', it is rightly called animal. For nothing can walk except an animal. Further, under species are individuals, as Cicero and Virgil under man, of which individuals the genus of the species can be predicated. For if you ask, 'What is Cicero?', you would rightly say animal. Genus therefore is named of the species, and of differences, and of accidents, and of properties, and of individuals.

passages.original: Ita ergo species de proprio prædicatur ut pari. Sed quoniam sub speciebus sigillatim individua sunt : individua autem vocamus quæ in nullas species,nequeinaliquasjam aliaS partes dividi possunt, ut est Cato, vel Plato, vel Cicero, et quidquid hominum singulorum est: hos enim in nullis partibus dividis, ut animal in species, hominem scilicet, atque equum, hominem qunque ipsum specialem,etsingulos circumplectentem, in Catonem, Platonem.
passages.english: Thus, then, species is predicated of a property as of an equal. But since under species are individuals one by one—and we call individuals those things which cannot be divided into any species, nor any longer into any other parts, such as Cato, or Plato, or Cicero, and whatever single man there is: for these you do not divide into any parts, as [you divide] animal into species, namely man and horse, and man himself, the specific one that embraces individuals, into Cato, Plato,
passages.notes: The sentence is incomplete; it continues in the following passage.

passages.original: Ila individua quae ad unitatem dicuntur,cunctis superioribus supposita sunt, ut genus, species, differentia, ad propria, vel accidentia, quamvis ad se invicem dici possunt, ad individua tamen sequaliter praedicantur, ut superius demonstratum est.Individua vero, quoniam sub se nihil habent ubi secari distribuique possint, ad nihil aliud praedicantur, nisi ad seipsa quae singula atque una sunt. Atque hoc est quod ait Eorum quæ dicuntur alia ad unitatem dicuntur,sicutomnia individua,ut est Socrates, et hoc et illud. Alia quae ad multitudinem, ut sunt genera, et species, et differentiæ, et propria, et accidentia. Haec enim communiter non unius propriae appellationissunt.Simile est acsi diceret : Hæc enim communiterad plurima praedicantur, non ad unitatem sicut individua.
passages.english: Those individuals which are predicated of a single thing are placed beneath all the higher [terms], such as genus, species, difference, properties and accidents, which, although they can be predicated of one another, are nonetheless predicated equally of individuals, as was shown above. Individuals, however, since they have nothing beneath them into which they could be divided and distributed, are predicated of nothing else except themselves, which are single and one. And this is what he says: "Of the things that are predicated, some are predicated of a single thing, as are all individuals, for example Socrates, and this and that. Others are predicated of a multitude, as are genera, and species, and differences, and properties, and accidents. For these belong in common [to many], and are not the proper appellation of one [thing]." It is as if he were saying: "For these are predicated in common of very many things, not of a single thing as individuals are."
passages.notes: "Ila" read as "Illa"; "ad propria" probably for "at propria" or "et propria"; "sequaliter" read as "aequaliter". The construction of the first sentence is loose in the Latin.

passages.original: Distant autem, quod quamvis utraque ari plurima praedicentur,et id eo quod quid sit genus tamen praedicatur ad res specie differentes,species vero dicitur ad res tantum numero differentes,quod Porphyrius s:c demonstrat:
passages.english: They differ, however, in that, although both are predicated of very many things, and in respect of what something is, genus nevertheless is predicated of things differing in species, whereas species is said of things differing only in number, which Porphyry demonstrates thus:

passages.original: Sin vero converteris,et prius definitionem, postea rem dixeris, ut si dicas, animal quod fuerit rationale, mortale, risus et disciplinae perceptibile homo est,hæc quoque vera est: ita semper ut definitiones verae sint,neque plus, neque minus in dfiniLionibus oportet aptari,sed aequaliter definitiones convenienterque disponi. Quod Porphyrius scilicet nou ignorans ait,se neque plus, neque minus tiffecisse generis definitionem.Et Fabius : Sequitur inquit despeciedisputare.Dic,inquam,quid sequitur? Et sequitur; Hic (ut opinor) ordo est:
passages.english: But if you reverse it, and state the definition first and the thing afterwards, as if you were to say, 'An animal which is rational, mortal, capable of laughter and of learning is a man,' this too is true: so that, for definitions always to be true, neither more nor less must be fitted into the definitions, but definitions must be arranged equally and fittingly. Porphyry, certainly not unaware of this, says that he has made the definition of genus neither more nor less [than it should be]. And Fabius said: 'Next it follows to discuss species.' 'Tell me,' I said, 'what follows?' And it follows; this, I think, is the order:
passages.notes: 'tiffecisse' read as 'effecisse'. 'Et sequitur' is abrupt; possibly the text quoted from Porphyry is meant.

passages.original: Speciem esse,qu;e ad plurimas resnumero differentes in eo quod quid sit prædicetur.Sed hæc definitio subalternis speciebus nunquam conveniet.Illaeenim quæ subalternæ sunt species, possunt etiam pro generibus accipi, si ad subjectaprsedicentur.Quod si possunt pro generibus accipi,cum progeneribus acceptae fuennt,non tantum ab plurimas res numero,sed etiam specie dilferenles prædicabuntur, quippe cum sunt genera.Sed quia hoc in magis speciebus nonevenitutaliquandodespeciedifferentibus praedicentur, haee definitio posterior solius magis speciei definitio est,et eam caeterae subalternae species excludunt atque rejiciunt,quod Porphyrius ita demonstrat.Sed hæc definitio ejus speciei est, quæ magis species dicitur. Aliæ vero definitiones erunt etiam illarum quae non sunt magis species,horum ergo ipsam subscriptionem demonstrationemque clarius seipsum dicere prornittit cum dicit:
passages.english: 'Species is what is predicated of many things differing in number in respect of what something is.' But this definition will never fit subaltern species. For those that are subaltern species can also be taken as genera, if they are predicated of what is subject to them. And if they can be taken as genera, when they have been taken as genera they will be predicated not only of many things differing in number, but also of things differing in species, since they are genera. But because it does not happen in the most special species that they are sometimes predicated of things differing in species, this latter definition is the definition of the most special species alone, and the other subaltern species exclude and reject it, which Porphyry shows thus: 'But this definition is of that species which is called most properly species. Other definitions will be also of those which are not most properly species.' He therefore promises to state their description and demonstration more clearly himself when he says:
passages.notes: 'magis species' rendered as 'most special/most properly species' (translating Greek eidikōtaton). 'ab plurimas' read as 'ad plurimas'. Passage ends with an unquoted lemma.

passages.original: Quod si ita est, non est dubium quin genus quoqne generis illius,quod ad illud ad quod species praedicabatur,poterat praedicari, etiam id quoque de eo de quo species etgenus speciei prædicabatur,prædicari posse. Nam si quis dicat Ciceronem esse hominem, cum animal hominis genus sit, non erit absurdum Ciceronem animal prædicari, et cum animalis ipsius substantia genus sit,non erit inconveniens Ciceronem substantiam praedicari, quoniam quae supersunt de subterioribuspraedicantur,etquce subteriora sunt si qua alia sibi subteriorahabeant,illud primum genus habebunt etiam ista subteriora,et de his non inconvenienter praedicabitur.
passages.english: If this is so, there is no doubt that the genus of that genus too, which could be predicated of that of which the species was predicated, can also itself be predicated of that of which the species and the genus of the species were predicated. For if someone says that Cicero is a man, since animal is the genus of man, it will not be absurd for Cicero to be predicated [as] animal; and since substance is the genus of animal itself, it will not be unfitting for Cicero to be predicated [as] substance, since the things that are above are predicated of the lower ones, and if the things that are lower have any others lower than themselves, these lower ones too will have that first genus, and it will be predicated of them not unfittingly.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected silently (quoqne for quoque, etgenus, subterioribuspraedicantur, etc.). The first sentence is syntactically awkward in the Latin ('quod ad illud ad quod'); translated according to the evident sense.

passages.original: : et ista quatuor sibi proportionaliter sunt.Eodem enim modo ex materia et figuraspeciesuniuscujusqueillius fictionis formataest,quemadmodum ex genereetdifferentiisspecies cujuscunque illius animanlis inanimantisve formatur,quod Victorinus scilicetintellexisse minus videtur.Nani quod Porphyrius ἄλογον dixit,id est proportionaJe,ille sic accepit quasi ἀνάλογον diceret, id est irrationaliter.Atque ideo in loco ubi habet hoc modo scriptum : Omnes namque res ex forma et materia consistunt,ipsa autem forma irrationalis est,tollendum est irrationale,Etsubterius paulu lum ubi habetur:Jam omnes genus simile materiæ est,et consistit irrationale, tollendum est irrationale,et ponendum est proportionale, ut sit,et consistit proportionaliter.
passages.english: : and these four are in proportion to one another. For the species of each such fashioned thing is formed from matter and shape in the same way as the species of any animate or inanimate thing is formed from genus and differences, which Victorinus, it seems, understood too little. For what Porphyry called ἄλογον, that is, 'proportional', he took as if he had said ἀνάλογον, that is, 'irrationally'. And therefore in the place where he has it written thus: 'For all things consist of form and matter, but the form itself is irrational', 'irrational' must be removed; and a little further down, where it reads: 'Now every genus is similar to matter, and consists irrationally', 'irrational' must be removed and 'proportional' put in, so that it reads 'and consists proportionally'.
passages.notes: The Greek terms appear reversed in the text as printed: the sense requires that Porphyry wrote ἀνάλογον ('proportional') and Victorinus took it as ἄλογον ('irrational'). Translated as printed, but the glosses follow the evident meaning. 'Jam omnes genus' presumably for 'Jam omne genus'.

passages.original: Illa vero alia bipes,vel grammaticus propria quidem sunt,sed converti non possunt.Nam grammaticus semper nomo,homo vero non semper grammaticus.Et econtrario homo semper bipes est, non econtra bipes semper homo est.Et hinnibile similiter magis proprium equi est.Nam eodem modo hæc proprietas ad suam speciem converti potest : nam si dicas quid estequus,hinnibile respondebis. Si,quid est hinnibile,equus prædicabitur. Sed quoniam de propriis dictum est,de accidentibus sequens tractatus habeatur.Tum Fabius : Definit Porphyrius accidens sic.
passages.english: But those others, 'biped' or 'grammarian', are indeed properties, but they cannot be converted. For a grammarian is always a man, but a man is not always a grammarian. And conversely a man is always biped, but not conversely is a biped always a man. And 'capable of neighing' likewise is more properly a property of the horse. For in the same way this property can be converted with its species: for if you say 'What is a horse?', you will answer 'capable of neighing'; if 'What is capable of neighing?', horse will be predicated. But since we have spoken about properties, let the following discussion be held about accidents. Then Fabius: Porphyry defines accident thus.
passages.notes: 'nomo' read as 'homo'. The grammarian example seems confused in the Latin (one would expect 'grammarian is not always a man' to be the non-convertible direction, as properties of a part of a species); translated as it stands.

passages.original: Differentia enim quadrupes in bovis, et in equi, et in canis specie est: et differentia rationalis hominis et angeli, species veronunquamaliis,nisisolissubsepositisindividuis praeest.Nunquam enim alia res homo est, nisi quod est individuum,ut est Socrates, et Plato, et Cicero. Unde fit ut sublata difIerentia,species quoque toll a- tur.Nam si sustuleris rationale, hominem sustuleris. Sin vero sustuleris speciem, differentia manet. Nam si sustuleris hominem rationalis angeli differentia manebit.Est vero etiam hæc differentia, quod differentia cum alia differentia jungipotest,utaliqua ex his species informetur.
passages.english: For the difference "four-footed" is found in the species of ox, of horse and of dog; and the difference "rational" [belongs to] man and angel. A species, however, is never set over anything else except only the individuals placed beneath it. For man is never anything else except what is an individual, such as Socrates, and Plato, and Cicero. Hence it comes about that if the difference is removed, the species too is removed. For if you remove rational, you will have removed man. But if you remove the species, the difference remains. For if you remove man, the difference rational will remain in angel. There is also this difference, that a difference can be joined with another difference, so that some species is formed out of them.
passages.notes: Text run together in the scan ("veronunquamaliis...", "toll a- tur") has been read as "vero nunquam aliis, nisi solis subsepositis individuis praeest" and "tollatur".
